title: What a hadith is
hookLine: a report of what the Prophet ﷺ said, did, or approved

lines: WHAT DID HE DO AT HOME?
cards: Someone once asked Aisha a plain, domestic question: what did the Prophet do at home? Not in the mosque, not on the battlefield. At home.
Her answer is preserved in Sahih al-Bukhari. He was busy serving his family, she said, and when the time for prayer came, he went out to pray.

That small answer has been carried, person to person and then book to book, so it can be heard today. A new block begins with that kind of report: what it is, how it travels, how it's tested. Today, the hadith.

teach.b: The Arabic word hadith is usually put into English as a report, or news.
In Islamic scholarship it names a report about the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and scholars sort those reports by what they carry. First, what he said.
In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet says the Muslim is the one from whose tongue and hand other Muslims are safe. One sentence, a whole ethic, in his own words as remembered. Second, what he did.
That's Aisha's answer: no command at all, only a description. People watched how he lived, so a deed reported becomes a teaching.

Third, what he approved, the easiest one to miss. Also in Bukhari: a companion who led prayers kept ending his recitation with one short surah, al-Ikhlas. When the people came back, they mentioned it to the Prophet.
He didn't say yes or no. He said: ask him why. The man said it describes the Most Merciful, and he loved to recite it.
And the Prophet said: tell him that Allah loves him. The approval is the teaching. His silence, or his yes, to something done in front of him is reported too.
Fourth, who gathers them. Sunni scholars collect reports of the Prophet carried through his companions.

Shia scholars also gather reports of the Prophet, and beside them the sayings of the Imams of his family, weighed through their own collections and methods. Both treat a report about him as a serious thing to carry.
So when a sentence starts with "the Prophet said", ask: said, did, or approved? And who carried it here?

how: Muslims read hadith in collections such as Sahih al-Bukhari, hear them quoted in Friday sermons and study circles, and Sunni and Shia scholars each gather and weigh reports through their own collections.

o: a report of what the Prophet said, did or approved
a ruling given by a judge in a Muslim court
a verse of the Qur'an, recited aloud in prayer

games.q: what a hadith carries — tap the pairs.
p: tongue and hand, and who is safe
tell him that Allah loves him

s: a hadith is only something the Prophet said
scholars count what he said, what he did, and what he approved.
Aisha described the Prophet serving his family at home
she said he was busy serving his family until the time for prayer.
Shia scholars gather no reports of the Prophet
they gather his reports, and also sayings of the Imams of his family.

games.q: a man leading prayer ends his recitation with al-Ikhlas every time. people mention it to the Prophet. what does he do first?
o: tell them to ask the man why.
games.why: he said: ask him why. the man loved that surah because it describes the Most Merciful, and the Prophet said: tell him that Allah loves him.

practice: Take today's hadith slowly: the Muslim is the one from whose tongue and hand others are safe.
Walk through yesterday with it, the moment your tongue wasn't safe for someone, a sharp text, a joke at someone's expense, and the moment your hands were a shelter, carrying, fixing, holding a door.
Don't grade yourself; just notice both. If you pray, you can ask for a safe tongue; if not, rest with the sentence.

wordCard.voice: Hadith. A report of what the Prophet said, did, or approved, carried by the people who saw and heard him. Today's word.

orig.note: a report, a piece of speech or news: in scholarship, a report about the Prophet.

carryVoice: Your line: a report. Said, did, or approved, and carried by someone. See you tomorrow.
